t: God Looks at Your Heart
v: When they had come, he looked at Eliab, and said, “Surely the LORD’s anointed is before him.”

But the LORD said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.”
Then Jesse called Abinadab, and made him pass before Samuel. He said, “The LORD has not chosen this one, either.”
Then Jesse made Shammah to pass by. He said, “The LORD has not chosen this one, either.”
Jesse made seven of his sons to pass before Samuel. Samuel said to Jesse, “The LORD has not chosen these.”

Samuel said to Jesse, “Are all your children here?” He said, “There remains yet the youngest. Behold, he is keeping the sheep.” Samuel said to Jesse, “Send and get him, for we will not sit down until he comes here.”
He sent, and brought him in. Now he was ruddy, with a handsome face and good appearance. The LORD said, “Arise! Anoint him, for this is he.”
b: Even the prophet Samuel could be influenced by outward appearance. As soon as he saw the tall Eliab, he concluded, “Surely the LORD’s anointed is before him.” But God immediately corrected his viewpoint: “Man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.” People tend to look at ability, education, looks, status, and achievements, but God first looks at whether a person’s heart fears and obeys him. Spiritual change is learning to move from a human point of view to God’s, no longer judging only with our eyes, but seeking what God truly values.

David was not even on the list of candidates his father Jesse put forward; he was out tending sheep. But in the places people cannot see, God had already seen him. The wilderness was not wasted time but the place where God shaped his life; shepherding was not an unnoticed job but the training ground where God prepared a king. God’s order of work is often life first, then relationships, then ministry. He didn’t first give David the throne and then shape his life; he first nurtured David’s faithfulness where no one was watching, and then entrusted him with greater responsibility.

So what matters most in life is not “how others see me” but “how God sees my heart.” We don’t need to prove ourselves by outward performance, and we shouldn’t be discouraged when others overlook us. What matters is letting Jesus be King in our hearts each day, taking God’s word as our standard, and obeying the Holy Spirit’s leading. When our hearts turn to God alone, even if no one sees us for the time being, God still sees; and in his time, he knows how to put those after his own heart in the right place.
a: Don’t judge people by appearance alone
Learn to see yourself and others through God’s eyes.
Be faithful in hidden places
Even when no one is watching, faithfully do what God has entrusted to you.
Build life first, then take on ministry
Don’t rush after a position; first let God shape a heart after his own.
q: If God today looked not at my outward performance but at my heart, what kind of heart would he see?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, help me stop looking only at outward appearance and stop living under other people’s eyes. Search my heart and remove my pride, self-centeredness, and comparison with others, and give me a humble heart that fears and obeys You. Even where no one sees, let me faithfully follow You. Let Jesus be King in me, and prepare me to be someone after Your heart whom You can use. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: “Man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart.”

t: When Lives Are Connected, the Church Grows Naturally
v: They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.
Fear came on every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles.
All who believed were together, and had all things in common.
They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need.
Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,
praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.
b: After the Holy Spirit came at Pentecost, the first church was born. What Luke records first is not how many organizations they built but four most basic things: the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and prayer. This shows us that the church is first of all a “community of life.” They built their lives on truth, prayed in the Spirit, had fellowship with Christ, and built relationships with one another. A truly healthy church has life first, then relationships, and finally ministry arises naturally.

The lives of these believers also truly entered into one another’s needs. They “distributed them to all, according as anyone had need,” and lived together day by day with one accord, with gladness and sincerity. This was not a forced abolition of private property; it was God’s love making people willing to share. When “mine” is no longer the center of life, we begin to see “ours”; when Jesus is King, people are willing to lay themselves down and look after one another. True unity is not that everyone has no differences, but that everyone centers on Christ and helps one another flourish in love.

Finally there is a very important sentence: “The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.” The real subject of church growth is the Lord. The disciples faithfully lived out truth, loved one another, prayed, worshiped, and bore witness, but it is God who saves people and makes the church grow. So building the church is not about manufacturing numbers by human methods, but about letting Jesus be King and the Holy Spirit reign, so that Christ’s life can be seen through the community. When lives are built up, relationships are built up, and the gospel is lived out, the Lord can naturally add more of the saved to the church.
a: Build a life connection with God
Persevere in reading Scripture, praying, and worshiping, and let truth enter daily life.
Build real spiritual relationships
Fellowship, care for, share with, and help one another flourish.
Let the Lord grow the church
Faithfully live out Christ and proclaim the gospel, and hand the results and the glory to God.
q: Am I merely “attending church activities,” or truly building lives of mutual love and mutual building up with my brothers and sisters?
pr: Dear heavenly Father, make us not only gather but truly become the body of Christ. Help us be rooted in truth, pray earnestly, love one another, and walk together in unity, laying ourselves down and letting Jesus be King among us. May we live out the life of Christ and build relationships that belong to God, so that more people see Jesus through us and receive the gospel, and all the glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: “The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.”

t: The Greatest Hope: Being with the Lord Forever
v: But we don’t want you to be ignorant, brothers, concerning those who have fallen asleep, so that you don’t grieve like the rest, who have no hope.
For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep in Jesus.
For this we tell you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will in no way precede those who have fallen asleep.
For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel and with God’s trumpet. The dead in Christ will rise first,
then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. So we will be with the Lord forever.
Therefore comfort one another with these words.
b: Paul does not say that Christians will not grieve in the face of death. He says we do not need to grieve “like the rest, who have no hope.” Parting is real, and tears are real, but death does not have the last word. Our hope rests on a fact of history that has already happened: “Jesus died and rose again.” Because Christ has conquered death, everyone who is in Christ has the hope of resurrection too. The cross tells us that death is real; the empty tomb tells us that death is no longer the end.

This passage lifts our eyes from today to the coming of the Lord. Paul says, “The Lord himself will descend from heaven,” the dead in Christ will rise, and all who belong to the Lord will meet him. The Christian’s true hope is not merely going someday to a beautiful place, but being with a Lord who loves us, forever. What is most precious about heaven is not the streets of gold or the gates of pearl, but Jesus himself. So the focus of our lives today should also be on Jesus: not on ourselves, not on others, not on circumstances, but on the One who died for us, rose for us, and is coming again.

“So we will be with the Lord forever.” This is the summit of the whole passage and the eternal hope of every believer. All our tears, pain, sickness, aging, and death today are temporary, but being with the Lord is forever. Since our destination is to be with Christ forever, we should let Christ be our life today, let Jesus be King in our hearts, and live out his love and holiness. When we turn from a temporary viewpoint to an eternal one, we can still have hope in the midst of parting, and still wait for the Lord in the dark night.
a: Hope in the Midst of Grief
You may weep, but do not despair, because Christ has risen.
See Today in Light of Eternity
Do not let temporary gains and losses decide the worth of your life.
Prepare to Meet Jesus
Let Jesus be King in your life today and live out the life of Christ.
q: If I truly believe that one day I will be with the Lord forever, how would my life look different today?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for raising Jesus Christ from the dead and giving us an eternal hope. When I face parting, loss, and death, lift my eyes above what is in front of me and fix them on the risen Lord. Help me treasure today, live out Christ, and be ready to meet Jesus, until I am with the Lord forever. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: “So we will be with the Lord forever.”

t: In Suffering, Still Trusting God
v: So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD, and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head.
He took for himself a potsherd to scrape himself with, and he sat among the ashes.
Then his wife said to him, “Do you still maintain your integrity? Renounce God, and die.”
But he said to her, “You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. What? Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” In all this Job didn’t sin with his lips.

Now when Job’s three friends heard of all this evil that had come on him, they each came from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite; and they made an appointment together to come to sympathize with him and to comfort him.
When they lifted up their eyes from a distance, and didn’t recognize him, they raised their voices, and wept; and they each tore his robe, and sprinkled dust on their heads toward the sky.
So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.
b: After losing his possessions and his children, Job now suffers terrible pain in his own body. It is worth noticing that Job did not know the heavenly background revealed in chapters one and two. He did not know why suffering had come to him, yet he chose not to abandon God. True faith is not “I will believe in God as long as he blesses me the way I want.” It is acknowledging that God is God even when we understand nothing at all. The deepest test of suffering is often not whether we can find answers, but whether we will still let God be God when there are none.

Job says, “Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?” This does not mean God delights in hurting people, nor that people should suppress their pain in suffering; Job will later weep, question, and pour out his heart to God just the same. The point of this sentence is that he refuses to put himself in God’s place and sit in judgment over him. Trusting God is easy when circumstances are smooth; holding on to God when life is shattered is what shows faith to be real. If our focus is only on circumstances, we easily ask “Why?” When our focus returns to God, we can go further and ask, “Even if I don’t understand right now, do I still trust him?”

Job’s three friends did something very beautiful at this moment: they sat with him “on the ground seven days and seven nights,” because they saw how great his grief was. The best comfort at that time was not explanation but presence. Some wounds cannot be healed with a single sentence; real love is willing to sit beside the one who suffers, to weep with him and walk with him through the night. People matter more than events, and relationships matter more than answers. Sometimes we do not need to rush to explain everything for God. We only need to let the love of Christ flow through our presence, so that the hurting know: you are not alone.
a: Trust When You Don’t Understand
No answer does not mean God has lost control.
Let God Be God in Suffering
You may weep and pour out your heart to him, but do not walk away from him.
Presence Matters More Than Answers
With those who suffer, preach less and simply be there more.
q: If God does not immediately change my circumstances, am I still willing to trust him and follow him?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, when I meet suffering I cannot understand, do not let me lose faith because of my circumstances. Even when I don’t know why, I still believe that You are God and that You are still in control. Give me also the compassionate heart of Christ, so that I may know how to sit with those who suffer, not hurrying to judge or to give answers, but walking with them in love. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: “Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?”

t: Don’t Run Ahead of God
v: After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple, Neco king of Egypt went up to fight against Carchemish by the Euphrates, and Josiah went out against him.

But he sent ambassadors to him, saying, “What have I to do with you, you king of Judah? I come not against you today, but against the house with which I have war. God has commanded me to make haste. Beware that it is God who is with me, that he not destroy you.”

Nevertheless Josiah would not turn his face from him, but disguised himself, that he might fight with him, and didn’t listen to the words of Neco from the mouth of God, and came to fight in the valley of Megiddo.
The archers shot at King Josiah; and the king said to his servants, “Take me away, because I am seriously wounded!”

So his servants took him out of the chariot, and put him in the second chariot that he had, and brought him to Jerusalem; and he died, and was buried in the tombs of his fathers. All Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah.

Jeremiah lamented for Josiah, and all the singing men and singing women spoke of Josiah in their lamentations to this day; and they made them an ordinance in Israel. Behold, they are written in the lamentations.
Now the rest of the acts of Josiah and his good deeds, according to that which is written in the LORD’s law,
and his acts, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.
b: Josiah was a God-fearing king who led Judah into revival, but this passage gives us a deeply sobering reminder: having obeyed God in the past does not mean we no longer need to seek him afresh today. Neco, king of Egypt, had not come to attack Judah, yet Josiah went out on his own to stop him. The author of Chronicles points out specifically that Josiah “did not listen to the words of Neco from the mouth of God.” The problem was not only a wrong military decision; it was that in this matter he did not listen to God. One of the greatest dangers in the spiritual life is that, because of past successes, we assume our present judgment must be right.

Even more striking is that God’s warning came through someone Josiah would never have expected: Neco, king of Egypt. This does not mean that everyone’s words are the word of God, but it reminds us that we must not reject a warning without examining whether God is in it simply because we dislike the messenger. A humble person is not someone without judgment, but someone who does not treat his own judgment as the highest authority. Letting God be God and letting people be people means letting go of “I must be right,” taking the Bible as our standard, and seeking the leading of the Holy Spirit in prayer.

Josiah did many good things in his life, yet in the end he paid a heavy price for one act of not listening. This reminds us that the spiritual path is not lived today on yesterday’s victories, but by following God every day. True service is not “what I want to do for God,” but “what God wants me to do today.” Sometimes God says “Go,” and we move forward boldly; sometimes God says “Stop,” and we humbly stop. Do not run ahead of God, and do not lag behind God. Let Jesus be King and follow the leading of the Holy Spirit; that is the safest road.
a: Seek God Afresh Every Day
Don’t make today’s decisions on the strength of past successes.
Listen Humbly to Warnings
Don’t refuse to examine a warning just because the messenger isn’t who you expected.
Don’t Decide for God
When God says go, go; when God says stop, stop.
q: Is what I am doing now truly what God wants me to do, or only what I think I should do?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, give me a humble and teachable heart, so that I do not rely on myself because of past experience and achievements. Help me to seek Your will every day, to take Your Word as my standard, and to be sensitive to the leading of the Holy Spirit. Keep me from running ahead of You or lagging behind You; let Jesus be King, and let me faithfully follow in Your footsteps. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: “I will listen to God’s word and follow his leading.”

t: God Uses What Is in Your Hand
v: Moses answered, “But, behold, they will not believe me, nor listen to my voice; for they will say, ‘The LORD has not appeared to you.’”
The LORD said to him, “What is that in your hand?” He said, “A rod.”
He said, “Throw it on the ground.” He threw it on the ground, and it became a snake; and Moses ran away from it.
The LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand, and take it by the tail.” He stretched out his hand, and took hold of it, and it became a rod in his hand.
“This is so that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you.”
Moses said to the LORD, “O Lord, I am not eloquent, neither before now, nor since you have spoken to your servant; for I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.”
The LORD said to him, “Who made man’s mouth? Or who makes one mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Isn’t it I, the LORD?
b: When Moses faced God’s call, the first thing he saw was not how great God is, but how inadequate he himself was: “They will not believe me,” and “I am slow of speech.” But God asked him, “What is that in your hand?” It was only an ordinary shepherd’s rod, yet when Moses placed it in God’s hand, it became a vessel that displayed God’s power. God does not necessarily give us more first; he asks us to first hand over what we already have. What matters is not “how much do I have,” but “am I willing to give it to God.”

Moses looked at his own eloquence, but God told him to look at the One who made the mouth: “Who made man’s mouth?” This is the shift in perspective that faith brings. Look at yourself and you see only limits; look at God and you see the limitless. True faith is not believing that I am impressive, but believing that the God who calls me is powerful. Serving is not proving “I can,” but admitting “I can’t, but God can.” When we let go of being our own king and let Jesus be King, the Holy Spirit can lead us down the road God wants us to walk.

What God looks for is not the most capable person, but the one who is willing to obey. Moses’ rod, his speech, even his limitations, can all be placed in God’s hand. When we return to our rightful place as human beings, let God be God, and stop gripping for results ourselves, we can experience “not I who do it, but the Lord who does it, and I follow along.” God can use ordinary people, ordinary gifts, and ordinary resources to accomplish his extraordinary purposes, so that in the end Jesus receives all the glory.
a: Don’t Fixate on Your Inadequacy
Turn your focus from “I can’t” to “God can.”
Give God What Is in Your Hand
Your time, gifts, abilities, and experience: let God use them all.
Obey and Begin to Act
Don’t wait until you are fully ready; take the first step in reliance on God.
q: If God asked me today, “What is in your hand?” what would I be willing to give him to use?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, I am willing to give You myself and everything in my hand. Help me to stop staring at my limits and to look up to Your limitlessness; not to rely on myself, but to obey the leading of the Holy Spirit and let Jesus be King in me. May You use my life to accomplish Your purposes, so that all the glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: God will use what is in my hand, and by him I can complete the task he has given me!

t: Not One Lost
v: See that you don’t despise one of these little ones, for I tell you that in heaven their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.
For the Son of Man came to save that which was lost.
“What do you think? If a man has one hundred sheep, and one of them goes astray, doesn’t he leave the ninety-nine, go to the mountains, and seek that which has gone astray?
If he finds it, most certainly I tell you, he rejoices over it more than over the ninety-nine which have not gone astray.
Even so it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.
b: Jesus said, “See that you don’t despise one of these little ones.” In God’s eyes every life is infinitely precious. A person’s worth is not determined by ability, position, or achievement, but by the fact that he is loved by God. The world tends to value people with ability and influence, but Jesus takes special care of the small, the weak, and the wounded. To follow Jesus is to change our point of view, turning from human eyes to God’s eyes, and despising no one.

When one of a hundred sheep goes missing, the shepherd goes to look for that one. This shows us that God’s love does not look only at the total number, but sees each individual life. To the shepherd, the lost sheep is not an acceptable loss but a life that must be recovered. Jesus actively seeks the lost, so true shepherding is not merely managing a group or getting work done, but following Jesus by actively seeking, caring for, and walking with people, and bringing the lost back to the Lord’s side.
The Father “is not willing that one of these little ones should perish,” and this should become our heart in serving others. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things.

Do not lose people in order to finish the ministry, and do not give up on someone just because he is hard to walk with. When we lay down self and let Jesus be King, the Holy Spirit can place the shepherd’s heart in us, so that we watch over one another, accompany one another, and build one another up. Building God’s divine order begins with cherishing every life God has entrusted to us: not one lost.
a: Cherish Every Person
See each life through the Father’s eyes.
Actively Seek the Lost
Don’t just wait; take the initiative to care, accompany, and restore.
People Matter More Than Tasks
Don’t only get things done; build lives and relationships.
q: Who is the lost, hurting, or overlooked person God wants me to reach out to and walk with today?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for treasuring every life and never giving up on anyone. Put Jesus’ shepherd heart in me, so that I see not only tasks but people, and want to accompany lives, not just finish work. Help me lay down self and let Jesus be King, and by the Holy Spirit to seek out, care for, and support those who are lost and weak, so that every life may be built up and made whole. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: The Father does not want even one to be lost, and by the Lord I will cherish and recover every life!

t: Rejected by People, Still Used by God
v: Then the children of Ammon were gathered together and encamped in Gilead. The children of Israel assembled themselves together and encamped in Mizpah.
The people, the princes of Gilead, said to one another, “Who is the man who will begin to fight against the children of Ammon? He shall be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead.”

The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, “Therefore we have turned again to you now, that you may go with us and fight with the children of Ammon. You will be our head over all the inhabitants of Gilead.”
Then the LORD’s Spirit came on Jephthah, and he passed over Gilead and Manasseh, and passed over Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah of Gilead he passed over to the children of Ammon.
b: Jephthah had once been rejected by his own brothers and driven from his home, but when the Ammonites attacked Israel, the elders of Gilead came back and asked him to be their leader. The very people who rejected him yesterday needed him today. This shows us that people’s rejection cannot determine our worth, and past experiences cannot determine our future.

Don’t keep living in “how others have treated me.” Turn your focus to “what God wants me to do now.” When our viewpoint turns from people to God, we can let go of the hurt and walk again into what God has entrusted to us.

Jephthah did not refuse today’s responsibility because of past wounds. True victory is not only that circumstances change, but that life is no longer controlled by the past. If we keep clinging to our wounded selves, we easily live in bitterness and self-protection; but when we lay down self and let Jesus be King, we can move from “what I have suffered” to “who God wants me to become.” God can even use our past wildernesses and setbacks to shape us into people who are more mature and better able to carry a mission.

Yet the key to Jephthah’s ability to carry that mission was not only his courage, but this: “Yahweh’s Spirit came on Jephthah.” In the end, God’s work does not depend on human ability but on God’s Spirit. When our limitations are placed in God’s hands, we become vessels he can use. Take the Bible as our standard, seek the leading of the Holy Spirit, and follow the life of Jesus, letting Jesus be King; not proving ourselves by our own strength, but letting God accomplish his work through us, so that all glory goes to him.
a: Let Go of Human Rejection
Don’t let past hurts limit your life today.
Courageously Take Up What God Entrusts
Stop dwelling in the past and rise to answer God’s call today.
Move Forward in the Holy Spirit
Not proving your ability, but relying on God to complete the mission.
q: Am I still bound by past rejection or hurt? What is God calling me to lay down today, and what to take up again?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, help me let go of past rejection and hurt, and no longer be limited by how people see me. I turn my focus back to You and let Jesus be King in me. Fill me and lead me, Holy Spirit, so that I rely not on myself but on Your power to take up what You have entrusted to me, and become a useful vessel in Your hand, so that all glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: The Spirit of Yahweh is upon me, and by God I will complete the task he has entrusted to me!

t: Say Less, Listen More to God
v: Guard your steps when you go to God’s house; for to draw near to listen is better than to give the sacrifice of fools, for they don’t know that they do evil.
Don’t be rash with your mouth, and don’t let your heart be hasty to utter anything before God; for God is in heaven, and you on earth. Therefore let your words be few.
For as a dream comes with a multitude of cares, so a fool’s speech with a multitude of words.
When you vow a vow to God, don’t defer to pay it; for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay that which you vow.
It is better that you should not vow, than that you should vow and not pay.
b: When we come before God, the Preacher’s first reminder is not “speak more” but “draw near to listen.” True worship is not impressing God with many words, but listening to him with a heart of reverence. We easily come before God carrying our own ideas, hoping he will do what we want; but Scripture reminds us, “God is in heaven, and you on earth.” Humility is returning to our rightful place as human beings, letting God be God, and not rushing to make decisions for him. Listen to God first, then respond to him; seek the leading of the Holy Spirit first, then begin to act.

“Don’t be rash with your mouth, and don’t let your heart be hasty to utter anything.” Our words often reveal the true condition of our hearts. When self is king, we are quick to express ourselves, quick to defend, quick to prove ourselves; when Jesus is King, we learn to be quiet, to listen, and to discern. This is not to say we should not think, but that we should not decide everything by ourselves. Many problems in life and relationships come not from saying too little but from speaking too fast, before we have heard clearly. The less of our own voice, the more sensitive we become to God’s voice.

God also takes seriously the words we have spoken: “Pay that which you vow.” True godliness is not only in the feelings of our mouths but in faithfulness in daily life. When we say “I am willing” to God, we should carry it out in life; when we receive truth, we should obey it. Moving from “hearing” to “believing” and from “believing” to “practicing,” truth can truly change a life. What pleases God is not someone who speaks beautifully, but someone who hears his word and faithfully obeys it.
a: Listen Before You Speak
Be quiet in prayer and seek God’s heart first.
Be Slow to Speak
Don’t rush to defend or prove yourself; let Jesus be King in your heart.
Do What You Say
Keep faithfully every promise you make to God and to people.
q: When I come before God, do I keep telling him what I want, or do I truly quiet myself to listen to what he wants to say to me?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, give me a humble and quiet heart, so that when I come before You I do not rush to speak but first listen for Your voice. Help me lay down my own opinions, let Jesus be King, and be sensitive to the leading of the Holy Spirit; and help me be faithful to my commitments and live out in practice the truth I have heard. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will draw near to listen to God’s voice and faithfully obey his word!

t: Living in Victory in Christ
v: As therefore you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him,
rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, even as you were taught, abounding in it in thanksgiving.
Be careful that you don’t let anyone rob you through his philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the elemental spirits of the world, and not after Christ.
For in him all the fullness of the Deity dwells bodily,
and in him you are made full, who is the head of all principality and power.
In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made with hands, in the putting off of the body of the sins of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ,
having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.
You were dead through your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh. He made you alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses,
wiping out the handwriting in ordinances which was against us. He has taken it out of the way, nailing it to the cross.
Having stripped the principalities and the powers, he made a show of them openly, triumphing over them in it.
b: Paul says, “As therefore you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him.” Believing in Jesus is not merely accepting a religion; it is entering a brand-new life. Like a tree, what determines whether it can survive wind and rain is not the foliage outside but the roots within. Christians must likewise be “rooted and built up in him”: let Jesus be the foundation of life, let his Word be our standard, and let the Holy Spirit guide our path each day. Keep the focus on Jesus, not on yourself, not on others, not on circumstances; the deeper the roots, the steadier the life.

Paul repeatedly emphasizes “in him.” All the fullness of God is in Christ, and “in him you are made full.” The gospel is not about improving the old life through our own effort, but about being united with Christ and receiving his new life. The cross means the old self died with Christ, and the resurrection means we were made alive together with him. So real change is not “I will become more capable,” but “it is no longer I, but Christ who lives in me.”
When we lay down self as king and let Jesus be King, we no longer live by our own limited resources but in the fullness of Christ.

The cross is also the sign of Christ’s complete victory. God forgave all our trespasses, wiped out the record that stood against us, “nailing it to the cross,” and through the cross triumphed over all principalities and powers. So Christians do not strive by their own effort to win a victory; we live standing in the victory Christ has already won. The old self died with Christ, and the new self lives with Christ; it is not that we win by ourselves, but that the victorious Christ lives in us.
When Jesus is King, we can live out a new life by the Holy Spirit and give all the glory to him.
a: Be Rooted in Christ Every Day
Read God’s Word daily, draw near to God, and walk in the Lord.
Live in Christ
Don’t change yourself by your own effort; let Christ’s life be lived out from within.
Stand in the Victory of the Cross
Don’t be ruled by sin, accusation, or circumstances; live by faith in the victory Christ has already accomplished.
q: Today am I living by my own ability, or am I rooted and built up in Christ, letting Jesus be King in me?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, thank You for giving me new life in Christ and making me full in him. Help me to be rooted and built up in Christ every day, with a firm faith. Help me lay down self and no longer live by my own limited strength, but let Jesus be King in me and live out the life of Christ by the Holy Spirit. Let me stand in the victory the cross has already won, walk with the Lord all my life, and give all glory to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I am rooted and built up in Christ, firm in faith; in him I am made full!

t: A Good Word Brings Life
v: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
The tongue of the wise commends knowledge, but the mouths of fools gush out folly.
The LORD’s eyes are everywhere, keeping watch on the evil and the good.
A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but deceit in it crushes the spirit.
A fool despises his father’s correction, but he who heeds reproof shows prudence.
In the house of the righteous is much treasure, but the income of the wicked brings trouble.
b: A single sentence can put out a fire or fan it into flame. “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” When others treat us with anger, the old self’s instinct is to hit back at once, answering pride with pride, and usually both sides lose. But when we lay down self, stop fighting to win or to get the last word, and let Jesus be King in our hearts, we can answer pride with humility and defuse conflict with gentleness. True victory is not talking the other person down, but not letting anger control us.

“A gentle tongue is a tree of life, but perverseness in it crushes the spirit.” Words are not just sounds; they shape lives. One word of encouragement can help a discouraged person stand up again; one word of humiliation can leave a scar in someone’s heart for a very long time. So before speaking, ask: is this word meant to prove myself or to build up the other person?

When our focus is no longer on ourselves but on Jesus and the good of others, our mouths can become an outlet of blessing. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things; don’t wound a precious life just to win an argument over who is right.

Wisdom is shown not only in speaking well but also in being willing to be taught. “He who heeds reproof gains prudence.” Pride makes us defensive the moment we are reminded; humility makes us willing to see our own problems. When others point out our shortcomings, we need not rush to explain; we can first quietly examine ourselves before God. If it is true, humbly correct it; if it is not, entrust it to God. Speak gently, listen humbly, respond by the Holy Spirit, and both life and relationships will be built up together.
a: Respond Gently
When others are angry, don’t answer anger with anger.
Speak Words That Build Up
Before opening your mouth, ask: will this word bring life to someone?
Accept Correction Humbly
Don’t hurry to defend yourself; first see where you can change.
q: Today are my words crushing someone’s spirit, or are they becoming a “tree of life” for others?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, guard my heart and guard my mouth. When I face conflict, keep me from reacting in the flesh; let Jesus be King in me, and by the Holy Spirit help me speak gentle, wise, and edifying words. Give me also a humble, teachable heart, willing to receive correction and keep changing, so that my words bring life to others and build good relationships, and I give the glory to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: My answer will be gentle, turning away wrath; my tongue will be a tree of life!

t: Forgetting What Is Behind, Pressing Toward the Goal
v: that I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and the fellowship of his sufferings, becoming conformed to his death,
if by any means I may attain to the resurrection from the dead.
Not that I have already obtained, or am already made perfect; but I press on, that I may take hold of that for which also I was taken hold of by Christ Jesus.
Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before,
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
Let us therefore, as many as are perfect, think this way. If in anything you think otherwise, God will also reveal that to you.
Nevertheless, to the extent that we have already attained, let’s walk by the same rule. Let’s be of the same mind.
b: Paul’s greatest pursuit in life was not achievement, position, or human approval, but “that I may know him.” This “knowing” is not merely head knowledge about Jesus, but truly experiencing him in life: experiencing the power of his resurrection, and in suffering being conformed to his death. A true spiritual life is not just knowing more, but becoming more and more like Jesus. Jesus is my example, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide; the real goal of life is Christ.

Paul was already a mature apostle, yet he still said, “I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold.” A truly mature person does not feel he has already arrived, but the more he knows God, the more he sees he still needs to change. So he said, “forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before.” Forgetting what is behind does not mean denying the past; it means no longer being controlled by it. Past failures must not become today’s chains, and past successes must not become today’s pride. Let go of yesterday’s failures and also yesterday’s successes, and follow Jesus afresh today.

“I press on toward the goal” shows that life needs the right focus. A runner who keeps looking back can hardly move forward; a Christian who keeps looking at himself, at others, and at circumstances also easily loses direction. Focus on Jesus, not on yourself, not on others, not on circumstances.

We don’t need to compare ourselves with anyone; we only need to walk faithfully by the light God gives us today. “To the extent that we have already attained, let us walk by the same rule.” Let Jesus be King each day and take one more step by the Holy Spirit, and life will keep being renewed until we fulfill God’s calling for us in Christ.
a: Make Knowing Christ Your Life Goal
Don’t just know the truth; live out Christ.
Let Go of What Is Behind, Press On to What Is Ahead
Don’t be bound by past failures or satisfied with past successes.
Fix Your Eyes on Jesus and Run Straight
Don’t compare yourself with others; faithfully walk the road God has prepared for you.
q: What past failure, hurt, or success do I need to let go of so that I can focus more fully on pressing toward the goal in Christ?
pr: Dear Heavenly Father, I long to know Christ more deeply and to experience the power of his resurrection. Help me let go of past failures, hurts, and achievements, so that I am no longer bound by yesterday. I will let Jesus be King, and by the Holy Spirit press on toward what is ahead, fixing my eyes on Christ and running toward the goal, to fulfill Your calling on my life, so that all glory goes to You. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray. Amen.
dc: I will forget what is behind, press on to what is ahead, and run straight toward the goal!
